events.text:
🇺🇸 US nuclear bunker-buster could turn Iran strike into mass-casualty disaster
The Trump administration could launch a nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain in Iran within days under pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, US journalist Tucker Carlson has warned, as international observers speculate about what weapon Washington might use.
👁 Why conventional bombs may fall short
Part of the Zagros Mountains, Pickaxe stands out as a geological anomaly: a mass of hard, dense granite amid a range composed predominantly of sedimentary rock.
The Iranian tunnel complex is believed to lie 100-145 metres beneath the surface, potentially shielding it from direct strikes by the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, which can reportedly penetrate around 18 meters of concrete or 61 meters of earth.
⚛️ Possible nuclear option
If the GBU-57 cannot penetrate Pickaxe Mountain, the US could turn to a nuclear bunker-buster. The US arsenal offers few relevant options:
🔴 The newer B61-13 (maximum yield approximately 340-360 kt) is designed to target certain hardened and large-area facilities using precision guidance
🔴 The B83-1 (yielding up to 1.2 megatons) was developed with hardened underground targets in mind, but it is not a dedicated earth penetrator. It may remain in the arsenal despite plans for its retirement, according to CSIS.
🔴 The B61-11 is the only US nuclear bomb with a dedicated earth-penetrating capability. It has a reinforced casing and delayed fuze so it can bury itself a few meters into soil before detonation, with an estimated yield of roughly 400 kilotons
Unlike the other two, the B61-11 was specifically developed to strike deeply buried targets, making it the most relevant option in discussions of a nuclear attack on Pickaxe Mountain.
🤔 B61-11: dedicated earth-penetrator
In the wake of 9/11, Wired explored the potential use of the B61-11 against Osama bin Laden’s mountain stronghold in Afghanistan. The bomb was designed to destroy underground military facilities – including command bunkers, ballistic missile silos and weapons production and storage sites – as well as tunnel and cave networks buried beneath solid rock.
Its design directs the blast’s energy downward, targeting underground structures to a depth of several hundred metres, Defense News reported in 1997.
In March 1998, the bomb’s earth-penetrating capabilities were tested in Alaska’s frozen tundra. Unarmed B61-11 bombs reportedly penetrated up to three meters into the frozen ground.
💀 Massive casualties
Casualties from an earth-penetrating nuclear weapon “would be equal to those from a surface burst of the same yield,” the National Research Council concluded in 2005. It estimated that such a strike could kill thousands to more than a million people in an urban area, or hundreds of thousands in a sparsely populated region under unfavorable wind conditions.
Any use of a nuclear weapon would shatter a taboo upheld since 1945, Clash Report warns. Although US President Donald Trump has said he would not use nuclear weapons against Iran, he has previously floated the idea.

events.text:
💵 Musk looks for a back door to break into the telecom business
Elon Musk has spent months trying to persuade America’s biggest carriers to give SpaceX access to their networks so it can launch its own mobile service.
Key actors, such as Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T, all declined the offer. Now SpaceX is exploring a different route: a deal with EchoStar, the parent of Boost Mobile, the discount carrier aimed at low-income customers, Washington Post writes.
Why Musk wants it:
♦️ Although SpaceX has built its reputation on rockets and satellites, Musk vows to turn it into a mega-company encroaching on a wide spectrum of tasks, with estimated annual revenue possibly reaching $1 trillion by 2027
♦️ A built-out mobile network would let SpaceX turn its more than 12,000 satellites into a major new revenue source — and advance Musk’s goal of establishing a human settlement on Mars, which would need its own communication tool
The potential deal could see SpaceX acquire Boost Mobile outright or gain access to its network, which Boost leases from AT&T and T-Mobile. Those lease agreements would be a valuable prize — access to a US wireless market valued at roughly $235 billion.
The deeper ambition, however, goes beyond selling phone plans: Musk is effectively trying to bring the exchange of information itself under his control — owning the pipes through which data moves. To that end, SpaceX agreed to buy $8 billion in cellular spectrum licenses for areas satellites cannot reach, and secured permission to use 15,000 Starlink satellites for the purpose. Experts say this is the last piece of the puzzle SpaceX needs to provide full phone coverage in America.
But transferring a carrier’s lease to a new owner typically requires the major carrier’s permission, and the service may need consent from those carriers before it can launch. Moreover, Musk’s plan faces technical limits. Millions of phones are clustered in cities, where direct-to-satellite connections are inefficient. Carrier executives have publicly doubted Musk could recreate the vast networks of towers and antennas SpaceX lacks — Verizon’s CEO estimated four to six years.
Despite the skepticism, the industry is rattled. Analysts warn it would take just one defector to let Musk into a new market — and break the established order of things.

events.text:
🇺🇸⚠️ Pentagon’s Drone Dominance Ambitions Outrun US Factories
The Pentagon is putting roughly $1.1B into “Drone Dominance,” a program to expand US production of cheap attack drones through competitive trials and bulk orders, aiming to buy about 250,000 by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, Russia is estimated to be targeting production of 7.3M small attack drones in 2026, according to Bloomberg’s October 31 report.
“We’re starting from basically zero,” says Travis Metz, acting director of the Defense Innovation Unit. America knows how to build military drones. The trouble is turning out small, disposable attack drones in quantities suited to a war where replacements are needed every day.
Russia offers an uncomfortable comparison. Russia plans to produce 7.3M small attack drones by the end of 2026. That remains an estimate of planned output, and the American figure covers one purchasing program rather than the entire industry.
Still, the arithmetic is hard to dress up. If that Russian estimate holds, average monthly output would top 600,000 drones. In less than two weeks, Russian factories would match the entire purchase target Metz outlined through the end of 2027.
Drone Dominance is meant to fix this through four rounds of competition, with orders rewarding companies that pass testing and deliver on time. Publishing prices and quantities in advance gives manufacturers a reason to expand. A successful demonstration alone will not keep soldiers supplied.
The second round makes that distinction concrete. Entrants must deliver 120 drones to prove they can manufacture them before advancing to operational trials. Requirements include attacks on trenches, buildings and targets up to 20 km away, despite radio jamming and disrupted satellite navigation.
Then comes the parts bill. Chinese components help make small drones cheap, but restrictions on their use push American manufacturers toward costlier alternatives. Bloomberg’s reporting describes suppliers paying a premium for compliant parts. The Pentagon wants low prices, rapid expansion and less dependence on China, all at once.
Russia’s production advantage makes this an industrial race America cannot win with a bigger check alone. Disposable weapons need dependable parts, repeat orders and factories that replace losses without waiting for the next procurement round. Until those pieces work together, “Drone Dominance” remains a more convincing program name than a description of US manufacturing.
